one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban follows up his 'Grace Poe's residency' column with a Q&A on reader reactions, anchored on one central legal concern: the Maquiling v. Comelec (April 16, 2013) ruling that the use of a US passport after renouncing American citizenship effectively reverses the renunciation and disqualifies one from being elected to public office. He had concluded last Sunday that Poe's domicile of origin was Jaro, Iloilo; that California became her domicile by operation of law after her marriage; and that when she returned for good to the Philippines after the death of Fernando Poe Jr., she acquired a new domicile of choice -- with several acts in 2005 and early 2006 showing her intent to remain -- leading him to conclude she would surpass the 10-year residency requirement by Election Day, May 9, 2016. But a pen-named emailer, Agueda Kahabagan, presented immigration records showing Poe arriving in the Philippines using a US passport on November 9, 2003, December 13, 2004, September 2005, March 11, 2006, July 5, 2006, July 23, 2007, October 5, 2008, May 21, 2009, and August 3, 2009, and departing on July 2, 2006, July 26, 2006, September 11, 2006, November 1, 2006, October 31, 2007, April 20, 2009, July 31, 2009, and December 27, 2009 aboard PAL Flight 112 -- asking: under Maquiling, is Poe disqualified? An anonymous reader replies that Poe renounced her American citizenship in October 2010 -- after her last US-passport use on December 27, 2009 -- and has not used it since. CJ's analysis: if the anonymous reader is factually correct, Maquiling will not affect Poe and her residency still surpasses the 10-year requirement; if he is wrong, all Poe needs to do is renounce again her American citizenship before filing her COC, since Maquiling saw nothing wrong in executing more than one renunciation affidavit. The use of a foreign passport after renouncing foreign citizenship does not divest Filipino citizenship regained by repatriation under the Dual Citizenship Law. Residency is not interrupted by taking a renunciation or allegiance oath -- Japson v. Comelec (Jan 19, 2009); even foreigners may establish Philippine domicile -- Cordora v. Comelec (Feb 19, 2009). Reader Andrew Ramoso asked why the Constitution uses 'resident of' when it means 'domiciliary of' -- CJ replies that the law has its own interchangeable technical words, just as medicine has tongue-twisting terminologies better memorized by physicians scribbling seemingly inscrutable prescriptions. To those who asked whether CJP is campaigning or voting for Poe: that is a 'misleading question' -- it assumes a fact not in existence, since Poe has not decided whether to run or for what position. His columns are objective legal views, not political endorsements. CJ makes his election choices based on: (1) whether there is a candidate, (2) for what position, (3) their platform, and (4) the opposing candidates and their platforms.
